item.mechanism: Formation of a stable, continuous protective oxide film via tribo-oxidation reduces wear depth by shielding the metallic substrate from direct mechanical contact.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy produced by spark plasma sintering (SPS)
item.operating_conditions: Reciprocating wear test, atmospherical conditions, temperatures of 800 °C and 900 °C
item.supporting_observation: For the samples tested at 800 °C and 900 °C, an almost fully oxide-covered surface can be observed, which is relatively smooth and exhibits some grooves. The decrease in wear depth proves the protection of the underlying material by tribo-oxidation and the formaton of a stable oxide film.
item.scope_limits: Mechanism not dominant at room temperature and 500 °C where oxides are rough, inhomogeneous, and continuously removed; not tested under non-atmospherical conditions or sliding wear.
item.alternatives_considered: Abrasive wear of oxides and continuous formation/removal of oxides observed at lower temperatures.
quotes: The decrease in wear depth proves the protection of the underlying material by tribo-oxidation and the formaton of a stable oxide film.
For the samples tested at 800 °C and 900 °C, an almost fully oxide-covered surface can be observed, which is relatively smooth and exhibits some grooves.
The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions.

item.mechanism: High cooling rates during inert gas atomisation suppress decomposition and segregation, resulting in a fine distribution of two bcc phases which enhances hardness and wear resistance.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 feedstock powder and SPS samples
item.operating_conditions: Inert gas atomisation with high cooling rates; subsequent SPS processing at 1050 °C for 10 min
item.supporting_observation: Due to the high cooling rates during the atomisation process and hence fast solidification, a microstructure with a finer distribution of the phases occurs in comparison to arc-melted samples of the same alloy.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for arc-melted samples which show coarser structures; SPS processing introduces a σ-phase not present in the as-cast state.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of fcc phase and elemental segregation typical of casting processes.
quotes: Due to the high cooling rates during the atomisation process and hence fast solidification, a microstructure with a finer distribution of the phases occurs in comparison to arc-melted samples of the same alloy.
Due to the formation of the additional phase and a microstructure with a fine phase distribution, a high microhardness of 750 ± 17 HV0.5 was determined.
The fast cooling rate during atomisation suppresses the segregation of the melt and hence the precipitation of an fcc phase.

item.mechanism: Precipitation of a tetragonal σ-phase during SPS processing increases microhardness and wear resistance compared to arc-melted counterparts.
item.operating_conditions: Spark plasma sintering at 1050 °C for 10 min with passive cooling
item.supporting_observation: In comparison to the same alloy produced by arc-melting, a distinct increase in the hardness occurs due to the formation of the additional σ-phase and a microstructure with a finer phase distribution.
item.scope_limits: σ-phase may dissolve upon subsequent heat treatment and relatively fast air cooling; not tested for long-term stability at high temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Dissolution of σ-phase observed in other studies with heat treatment.
quotes: In comparison to the same alloy produced by arc-melting, a distinct increase in the hardness occurs due to the formation of the additional σ-phase and a microstructure with a finer phase distribution.
Additional diffraction peaks can be assigned to a tetragonal σ-phase.
The influence of the additional σ-phase has to be investigated in subsequent studies.

item.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures (500–650 °C), the formation of incomplete, rough oxide layers leads to intermittent protection and higher wear depth due to continuous oxide removal.
item.operating_conditions: Reciprocating wear test, atmospherical conditions, temperatures of 500 °C and 650 °C
item.supporting_observation: For both test conditions, rough and inhomogeneous oxides are formed, showing that a continuous formation and removal of oxides occur. This behaviour indicates an increasing stability caused by a rise in thickness and hence a protection of the underlying metallic material.
item.scope_limits: Mechanism transitions to stable protection above 800 °C; not applicable to room temperature where oxide coverage is partial.
item.alternatives_considered: Abrasive wear of oxides and interrupted oxide layer formation.
quotes: For both test conditions, rough and inhomogeneous oxides are formed, showing that a continuous formation and removal of oxides occur.
With a further increase in the test temperature, the content of the surface covered with oxides gradually increases.
With an increase in temperature from room temperature to 500 °C, a slight increase in the wear depth occurs, indicating a reduced wear resistance.

item.mechanism: Spinel phase formation (MgAl2O4 structure type) at very high temperatures contributes to the stability of the oxide layer and reduced friction.
item.operating_conditions: Reciprocating wear test, atmospherical conditions, temperatures of 800 °C and 900 °C
item.supporting_observation: The additional maxima can be assigned to a spinel (structure type MgAl 2 O 4 ). The intensity of the diffraction peaks increases for the sample tested at a maximum temperature of 900 °C.
item.scope_limits: Only observed at the two highest test temperatures; other oxides like TiO2 or Cr2O3 were not detected in this specific wear track analysis.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of TiO2 and (Al0.9Cr0.1)2O3 observed in previous oxidation studies at 900 °C.
quotes: The additional maxima can be assigned to a spinel (structure type MgAl 2 O 4 ).
The intensity of the diffraction peaks increases for the sample tested at a maximum temperature of 900 °C.
Phase analyses proved the formation of a spinel phase.

item.mechanism: The coefficient of friction (COF) decreases slightly with increasing temperature due to the smoothing effect of the stable oxide film and reduced mechanical interlocking.
item.operating_conditions: Reciprocating wear test, atmospherical conditions, temperatures from 22 °C to 900 °C
item.supporting_observation: With an increase in temperature up to 800 °C, the COF only slightly decreases. The lowest COF was measured for the highest test temperature of 900 °C, with an average value of 0.85.
item.scope_limits: High standard deviation occurs at temperatures up to 800 °C due to interrupted oxide layers; mechanism stabilizes only at 900 °C.
item.alternatives_considered: Abrasive wear of oxides and rough oxide surfaces causing higher friction at lower temperatures.
quotes: Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature.
The lowest COF was measured for the highest test temperature of 900 °C, with an average value of 0.85.
Furthermore, the COF decreases for the measurements at elevated temperatures.

item.mechanism: SPS processing enables dense bulk material production without grain coarsening, preserving the fine microstructure of the feedstock powder.
item.operating_conditions: Spark plasma sintering at 1050 °C for 10 min, compaction pressure 50 MPa
item.supporting_observation: No significant coarsening of microstructural features occurs during SPS processing. The overview image shows that a dense structure without porosity is produced.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to other sintering processes which may cause grain coarsening; specific to the SPS parameters used.
item.alternatives_considered: Casting defects like cavities, cracks, and elemental segregation.
quotes: No significant coarsening of microstructural features occurs during SPS processing.
The overview image shows that a dense structure without porosity is produced.
Furthermore, a low porosity and the absence of grain coarsening can be achieved for SPS samples.

item.mechanism: Alloying with titanium increases hardness, strength, and wear resistance, but high titanium contents can lead to embrittlement via complex phase formation.
item.operating_conditions: General alloy properties; as-cast state and various wear conditions
item.supporting_observation: Due to the high atomic radius, alloying with titanium can increase the hardness, the strength and the wear resistance. The highest wear resistance under various conditions... could be achieved for the alloy AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 with a medium titanium content.
item.scope_limits: Embitterment observed for high titanium contents due to complex phases; mechanism specific to medium Ti content.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of complex phases leading to brittle behavior at high Ti contents.
quotes: Due to the high atomic radius, alloying with titanium can increase the hardness, the strength and the wear resistance.
The highest wear resistance under various conditions, also in comparison with the bearing steel EN 1.3505, could be achieved for the alloy AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 with a medium titanium content.
Embrittlement was observed for high contents due the formation of complex phases.
